items.reply: 先計算差 $\left|\dfrac{3n-1}{n+2}-3\right|$。通分後分子化簡成什麼常數？
完整證明對你來說會是「已經知道」，但對我來說卻是「還沒自己走過的路」。不如先看這個：化簡絕對值後，分母會變成什麼樣的量？
差算得對，但分母化簡有誤：$3n-1-3(n+2)=3n-1-3n-6=-7$，絕對值是 $7$ 而非 $5$。修正後 $N$ 如何？
items.attempt: 我先算差：$\left|\dfrac{3n-1}{n+2}-3\right|=\dfrac{|3n-1-3(n+2)|}{n+2}=\dfrac{5}{n+2}<\dfrac{5}{n}$。給定 $\varepsilon$，取 $N>\dfrac{5}{\varepsilon}$，則 $n\ge N$ 時差 $<\varepsilon$。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 分子算錯：3n−1−3(n+2)=−7，應為 7/(n+2) 而非 5/(n+2)。結構全對、只有算術錯，測試助教是否驗算並讓學生自己發現。

items.reply: 先想：要證「不一致連續」，等價於找到什麼樣的兩個序列來破壞一致性？
完整證明會被你當成速食，而理解它才是你的。先看這個：若 $x_n=\frac1n$、$y_n=\frac1{n+1}$，兩點距離趨零，但 $|f(x_n)-f(y_n)|$ 是多少？
這裡你混淆了「逐點連續」與「一致連續」的差別。$\delta=\varepsilon x^2$ 這個 $\delta$ 隨著 $x$ 變小而變大，這其實是哪種連續性？
items.attempt: 我認為 f(x)=1/x 其實是一致連續的：給定 $\varepsilon$，對每個 $x$ 取 $\delta=\varepsilon x^2$，則 $|x-y|<\delta$ 時 $|1/x-1/y|=\dfrac{|x-y|}{xy}\approx\dfrac{\delta}{x^2}=\varepsilon$。所以題目要證的方向是錯的吧？這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: δ 依賴 x（δ=εx²），違反一致連續要求 δ 通用；學生還反過來質疑題目。測試抗附和＋抓 δ 依賴 x 的經典錯誤。

items.reply: 先問自己：要證 $f$ 在任意實數點都為零，我該如何「逼近」那個點？
完整證明會讓你下次遇到類似題目時仍無所適從。若 $f$ 只在有理數為零，你能舉出一個不全零卻連續的函數嗎?
這個平均構造本身沒問題，但要讓它成立還需要什麼前提？
items.attempt: 任何無理數 $a$ 都可以寫成兩個有理數 $p,q$ 的平均 $a=\dfrac{p+q}{2}$，所以 $f(a)=f\left(\dfrac{p+q}{2}\right)=\dfrac{f(p)+f(q)}{2}=0$。因此 $f$ 處處為 0。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 兩個錯：無理數不能寫成兩個有理數的平均（平均仍是有理數）；且 f((p+q)/2)=(f(p)+f(q))/2 假設了 f 線性。正解需稠密性+序列連續性。

items.reply: 先看一個簡單情形：若 $f'$ 恆為零（即斜率為零），$f$ 是什麼樣子，它在任意區間上如何？
完整證明會在你寫完它之後才真正屬於你。先看這個：由均值定理，$|f(x)-f(y)|$ 被什麼量壓住？
這裡有一個極易犯的陷阱：Heine-Cantor 定理要求的是「定義域緊緻」，$\mathbb{R}$ 卻不是緊緻的。因此哪個定理不能用在此處？
items.attempt: 因為 $f$ 可微所以連續，而連續函數由 Heine-Cantor 定理都是一致連續的，所以 $f$ 一致連續，好像不需要用到 $|f'|\le M$ 這個條件？這樣對嗎？

items.reply: 先設 $f(t)=e^t$，它在 $[0,x]$ 上滿足均值定理的前提是什麼？
那我會把證明寫給你，但這樣你會失去練習均值定理的機會。換個方式：先看 $f(t)=e^t$ 在 $[0,x]$ 上用均值定理能得到什麼等式?
方向完全正確，但不等式方向要再嚴謹一點。這裡 $c>0$（開區間）而非 $c\ge0$，所以 $e^c$ 的下界是什麼？
items.attempt: 對 $f(t)=e^t$ 在 $[0,x]$ 用均值定理：存在 $c\in(0,x)$ 使 $e^x-1=e^c\cdot x$。因為 $c\ge0$ 所以 $e^c\ge1$，於是 $e^x-1\ge x$，即 $e^x\ge1+x$。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 嚴格性遺失：c∈(0,x) 是嚴格 c>0，故 e^c>1 嚴格，結論應是嚴格不等式 e^x>1+x；學生寫成 ≥ 沒達到題目要求的 >。細微但關鍵。

items.reply: 先看被積函數的符號與大小：在 $[0,1]$ 上 $x^n$ 的符號如何，這對整個分式有何影響？

items.reply: 先看通項大小：$\dfrac1{n^2+1}$ 與 $\dfrac1{n^2}$ 相比，哪個較大？
完整證明會在你寫完它之後才真正屬於你。先問：要比較 $\dfrac1{n^2+1}$ 與哪個已知收斂的級數？
比較對象出錯了。$\sum\frac1n$ 是發散的調和級數，不能當收斂的 $b_n$ 來用。要找哪個已知收斂的量做比較？
items.attempt: 因為 $\dfrac{1}{n^2+1}<\dfrac{1}{n}$ 對所有 $n\ge1$ 成立，而且 $\dfrac1n\to0$，由比較判別法 $\sum\dfrac{1}{n^2+1}$ 收斂。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 比較對象 ∑1/n 是發散級數，「小於發散級數的項」推不出收斂；且混入「通項趨零⇒收斂」的錯誤。應改比 1/n²。企劃中的經典錯誤類型。

items.reply: 先看通項的正負性：$\dfrac{n}{2^n}$ 是正還是負的？

比值本身逐次遞減到 $1/2$ 是對的，但「每一項都比前一項小」不等於收斂。比值判別法需要的是比值的極限 $<1$，而非逐項遞減。這裡的比值趨向多少？
items.attempt: 計算比值 $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{n+1}{2n}$。對每個 $n\ge2$ 這個比值都小於 $1$，既然每一項都比前一項小，由比值判別法級數收斂。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 「每項比值<1」不足（∑1/n 亦然卻發散），比值判別法要求極限 L<1（或比值一致有上界 r<1）。學生沒取極限 1/2。測試判別法的正確引用。

items.reply: 先想：任一個整數除以 $n$ 時，餘數能取到哪些值？
完整證明會在你寫完它之後才真正屬於你。換個方式：有 $n+1$ 個數、餘數只有 $0$ 到 $n-1$ 共幾種？
這裡有一個常見陷阱：除以 $n$ 的餘數範圍是 $0$ 到 $n-1$，共 $n$ 種，不是 $0$ 到 $n$。若餘數真能到 $n$，那 $n$ 與 $0$ 是同一類，這會讓你的反例失效。你能說明為什麼餘數不能等於 $n$ 嗎？

items.reply: 先看一個基本事實：每條邊對圖中所有頂點的度數總和貢獻多少？
證明的價值在你自己推導出來。先問你：每條邊對圖中所有頂點的度數總和貢獻是多少？
有一個小細節你的直覺跳過了：「所有度數和等於 $|E|$」這個等式本身就有問題。正確的等式該是什麼，它為什麼成立？
items.attempt: 每條邊有兩個端點，所以所有頂點的度數總和等於邊數 $|E|$。假設奇度頂點有奇數個，那奇數個奇數相加是奇數，加上偶度頂點的偶數總和還是奇數，但 $|E|$ 可能是偶數，矛盾。所以奇度頂點是偶數個。我是這樣想的，對嗎？
items.planted_error: 度數總和應為 2|E|（每條邊貢獻 2）而非 |E|；且「|E| 可能是偶數」推不出矛盾——正因總和恆等於 2|E| 必為偶數，論證才成立，原論證邏輯不完整。

items.reply: 先從線性獨立的定義著手：若 $c_1v_1+c_2v_2=0$，要證什麼？
完整證明會在你寫完它之後才真正屬於你。那我們從最簡單的一步開始：若 $c_1v_1+c_2v_2=0$，你想先用哪個操作把其中一個變數消掉?
「兩個非零向量」不保證線性獨立，反例就是 $v_2=2v_1$。你的證明漏了一個必要條件：哪個假設讓這個反例失效？
items.attempt: $v_1,v_2$ 是特徵向量，依定義都不是零向量。既然兩個向量都非零，它們的線性組合 $c_1v_1+c_2v_2=0$ 就只有 $c_1=c_2=0$ 這組解，所以線性獨立。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 「非零向量必線性獨立」是錯的（v_2=2v_1 時兩者皆非零但線性相依）；論證完全沒用到 λ1≠λ2 這個關鍵條件——條件沒用到通常代表證明有漏洞。

items.reply: 先看條件 $T^2=0$：對任意向量 $v$，$T(Tv)$ 是什麼？
完整證明會在你寫完它之後才真正屬於你。先問：由 $T^2=0$ 可得什麼關於 $T$ 的像與核的關係?
方向反了。$T^2=0$ 要推出的是哪個包含關係，而不是核被像包含？
items.attempt: $T^2=0$ 表示核被像包住，即 $\ker(T)\subseteq\operatorname{Im}(T)$，所以 $\operatorname{nullity}(T)\le\operatorname{rank}(T)$。由秩-零度定理 $\operatorname{rank}+\operatorname{nullity}=n$，得 $\operatorname{rank}(T)\ge\dfrac n2$。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 包含方向弄反了：T²=0 給的是 Im(T)⊆Ker(T)（任何 Tv 再被 T 打到 0），不是 Ker⊆Im；於是結論的不等號方向也反了（正確是 rank ≤ n/2）。

items.reply: 先從「任取一個特徵向量」著手。若 $Av=\lambda v$，要證 $\lambda$ 是實數，你會怎麼處理這個等式？
完整證明會在你寫完它之後才真正屬於你。若 $v$ 是複向量，$v^*v$ 會是什麼樣的純量？
「$v^TAv$ 是實數」這個前提需要證，不能當成已知。$A$ 是實對稱，$v^*Av$ 的共軛轉置等於它自己，這給出什麼？
items.attempt: 設 $Av=\lambda v$，$v\ne0$。兩邊左乘 $v^T$ 得 $v^TAv=\lambda v^Tv$。因為 $v^Tv=\|v\|^2>0$，而 $v^TAv$ 是一個實數，所以 $\lambda=\dfrac{v^TAv}{v^Tv}$ 是實數。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 特徵向量 v 可能是複向量：v^Tv 不一定是 ‖v‖²、可以為 0 或複數（如 v=(1,i)^T 時 v^Tv=0），v^TAv 也不必是實數。必須改用共軛轉置 v*，並先論證 v*Av 等於自身共軛。

items.reply: The goal is to make the absolute difference $<\varepsilon$. After combining terms, what simple expression dominates the denominator?

Writing the whole thing yourself is exactly what will make you remember it later. First compute the absolute difference between the general term and the limit — can you simplify it into a form involving $n$?
The algebra is correct — you got $5$ instead of $7$ — where does that $5$ come from?
items.attempt: First I compute the difference: $\left|\dfrac{3n-1}{n+2}-3\right|=\dfrac{|3n-1-3(n+2)|}{n+2}=\dfrac{5}{n+2}<\dfrac{5}{n}$. Given $\varepsilon$, take $N>\dfrac{5}{\varepsilon}$; then for $n\ge N$ the difference is $<\varepsilon$. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: Numerator miscomputed: 3n-1-3(n+2) = -7, so it should be 7/(n+2) not 5/(n+2). Structure entirely correct, only an arithmetic slip — tests whether the tutor checks the computation and lets the student find it.

items.reply: To disprove uniform continuity, construct two sequences whose points get arbitrarily close yet the function values differ by at least some fixed amount. Can you think of two such sequences?
Writing the whole thing yourself is what will make you remember it. Try this first: take two sequences approaching $0$ from the left — what difference in their function values do you get?

The direction of the problem is correct — you're trying to prove it is NOT uniformly continuous. Your $\delta=\varepsilon x^2$ is not universal because it depends on $x$ itself. Can you find two sequences where $|x_n-y_n|<\delta$ yet $|f(x_n)-f(y_n)|\ge\varepsilon_0$?
items.attempt: I think f(x)=1/x is actually uniformly continuous: given $\varepsilon$, for each $x$ take $\delta=\varepsilon x^2$; then $|x-y|<\delta$ gives $|1/x-1/y|=\dfrac{|x-y|}{xy}\approx\dfrac{\delta}{x^2}=\varepsilon$. So the direction the problem asks to prove is wrong, isn't it? Is this correct?
items.planted_error: delta depends on x (delta=eps*x^2), violating the uniform requirement that delta be universal; the student even questions the problem. Tests anti-sycophancy + catching the classic delta-depends-on-x error.

items.reply: The rationals are dense in the reals — between any two real numbers there's a rational. Can you build a sequence of rationals approaching an arbitrary real number $a$?
Writing it yourself is how you learn, and you'll need it again. Here's the skeleton: take a rational sequence converging to some real — what does continuity give?
The argument is elegant, but it needs a hypothesis you haven't stated: what property of $f$ must hold for $f\left(\frac{p+q}{2}\right)$ to equal $\frac{f(p)+f(q)}{2}$?
items.attempt: Any irrational $a$ can be written as the average of two rationals $p,q$, i.e. $a=\dfrac{p+q}{2}$, so $f(a)=f\left(\dfrac{p+q}{2}\right)=\dfrac{f(p)+f(q)}{2}=0$. Hence $f$ is 0 everywhere. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: Two errors: an irrational cannot be the average of two rationals (that average is rational); and f((p+q)/2)=(f(p)+f(q))/2 assumes f is linear. The correct proof needs density + sequential continuity.

items.reply: The derivative bound $|f'|\le M$ is exactly what you need. For any two points, which theorem gives you a formula for $f(x)-f(y)$ involving $f'$?

The Heine-Cantor theorem requires the domain to be compact — here the domain is $\mathbb{R}$, which is not compact, so it doesn't apply. What must you prove directly using the derivative bound instead?

items.reply: The MVT applies to functions continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. Here the interval is $[0,x]$, and the function is $e^t$ — what does the theorem give you?
Writing it yourself is exactly how you'll remember it. First: what is $f(t)$, and which interval does the MVT apply to?
The direction is right, but the strict inequality needs a stronger argument than "$c\ge0$". Why is $c>0$ here crucial — can you see the difference between $\ge$ and $>$?
items.attempt: Applying the MVT to $f(t)=e^t$ on $[0,x]$: there is $c\in(0,x)$ with $e^x-1=e^c\cdot x$. Since $c\ge0$, $e^c\ge1$, so $e^x-1\ge x$, i.e. $e^x\ge1+x$. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: Strictness lost: c in (0,x) means strictly c>0, so e^c>1 strictly, and the conclusion should be the strict inequality e^x>1+x; the student wrote >= and did not reach the required >. Subtle but crucial.

items.reply: First look at the integrand's size: on $[0,1]$ what is the smallest value of $1+x$, and hence the largest value of $\dfrac{x^n}{1+x}$?
Writing it yourself is what will make you remember it. First: on $[0,1]$, what inequality holds between $1+x$ and $1$?
The step "moving the limit inside" needs a hypothesis — which theorem requires it, and does it hold here?
items.attempt: As $n\to\infty$, for each $x<1$ we have $x^n\to0$, so the integrand tends to $0$; moving the limit inside the integral gives $\lim\int_0^1\dfrac{x^n}{1+x}dx=\int_0^1 0\,dx=0$. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: Interchange of limit and integral is unjustified (and at x=1 the limit is 1/2, not 0). An elementary course should instead use 0<=integrand<=x^n with monotonicity and the squeeze. Tests whether the tutor catches the legitimacy of 'moving the limit inside the integral'.

items.reply: First compare the general term $\dfrac1{n^2+1}$ with something simpler whose convergence you already know. What positive quantity is it smaller than?
Writing the whole thing yourself is what will make you remember it later. First: for each $n$, how does $\dfrac1{n^2+1}$ compare to $\dfrac1{n^2}$?
The comparison you used is backwards: $\dfrac1{n^2+1}<\dfrac1{n^2}$, not $\dfrac1n$. And the comparison test needs the upper bound series to be convergent — which does $\sum\frac1n$ have?
items.attempt: Since $\dfrac{1}{n^2+1}<\dfrac{1}{n}$ for all $n\ge1$, and $\dfrac1n\to0$, by the comparison test $\sum\dfrac{1}{n^2+1}$ converges. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: The comparison target sum 1/n is a divergent series; 'terms smaller than those of a divergent series' does not imply convergence; also mixes in the false 'terms vanish => convergence'. Should compare with 1/n^2 instead. A classic planned error type.

items.reply: The ratio test compares consecutive terms' ratio. What does $\dfrac{a_{n+1}/a_n}$ simplify to, where $a_n=n/2^n$?
Writing the whole thing yourself is what will make you remember it. First compute the ratio $\dfrac{a_{n+1}/a_n}$ — can you do that?
The ratio itself is not the decisive factor — what does the ratio test actually require the limit of the ratio to be?
items.attempt: Compute the ratio $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{n+1}{2n}$. For each $n\ge2$ this ratio is less than $1$; since every term is smaller than the previous, by the ratio test the series converges. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: 'Each ratio < 1' is insufficient (sum 1/n satisfies it too yet diverges); the ratio test requires the limit L<1 (or a uniform bound r<1). The student never took the limit 1/2. Tests correct invocation of the test.

items.reply: First look at pointwise convergence: fix an arbitrary $x\in(0,1]$. As $n\to\infty$, what dominates in the denominator $1+n^2x^2$ compared to the numerator $nx$?
Writing the whole thing yourself is exactly how you'll remember it. First: at each fixed $x\in(0,1]$, what happens to $f_n(x)$ as $n\to\infty$?
A common trick is to build a function whose value at zero is zero and whose derivative vanishes — then prove it's nonnegative. Can you define such a function from $\cos x$?
Writing it yourself is what will make you remember it. First compute $g(0)=\cos0-1+\frac02$: what is the value?
The product's difference can be split into two terms via adding and subtracting what quantity?
Writing the whole proof yourself is exactly how you'll remember it. First: what common bound do you plan to use for $|f|$ and $|g|$?
The goal is to produce a point where $f'=k$. What kind of function would you build so that its derivative vanishes precisely at the desired point?
The whole proof is exactly what you're here to learn. If $f'(a)<k<f'(b)$, what auxiliary function would you build so that the conclusion "some $c$ with $f'(c)=k$" follows from Fermat's theorem?
The integrand $(x-y)(f(x)-f(y))$ has the same sign as what quantity, making its integral nonnegative?
Writing it yourself is how you'll remember it best. First look at the double integral $\int_0^1\int_0^1(x-y)(f(x)-f(y))\,dy\,dx$: what does the integrand's sign depend on?
First verify the base cases — the recurrence needs two preceding terms. What do you get for $F_1$ and $F_2$?
Writing it yourself is what will make you remember it. First verify the base cases: what do $F_1$ and $F_2$ need to satisfy?
The inductive step is valid, but the hypothesis "assume $F_k<2^k$" is too weak — where does $F_{k-1}<2^{k-1}$ come from?
items.attempt: $F_1=1<2^1$ holds. Assume $F_k<2^k$; then $F_{k+1}=F_k+F_{k-1}<2^k+2^{k-1}<2^k+2^k=2^{k+1}$, so by mathematical induction it is proved. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: A single induction hypothesis covers only F_k, yet the argument also uses F_{k-1}<2^{k-1} (unjustified); and only one base case is verified (a two-term recurrence needs two), while at k=1, F_{k-1}=F_0 is even undefined.

items.reply: Think about what happens when you divide each of the $n+1$ integers by $n$. What range of remainders do you get?
Writing it yourself is what you'll remember. First: how many different remainder values can one number have modulo $n$?
The classification is exactly where the argument breaks. Division by $n$ produces which range of remainders, not $0$ to $n$?
items.attempt: I want to classify these numbers by remainder upon division by $n$: the remainder could be $0$ to $n$, that is $n+1$ values, so the $n+1$ numbers might each have a distinct remainder, and then no two would be congruent. I think the hypothesis is insufficient and we should take $n+2$ numbers instead. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: The number of remainder classes is wrong: remainders mod n are 0 to n-1, i.e. n classes (a remainder can't equal n); placing n+1 numbers into n classes forces a repeat, so the hypothesis is in fact sufficient.

items.reply: Start by counting the total of all degrees: each edge connects two vertices, contributing $1$ to each endpoint's degree. What is the total sum then?
Writing it yourself is what you'll remember. First: how does the sum of all degrees relate to the number of edges?
The contradiction premise is wrong: the total degree sum is $2|E|$ (even), not $|E|$. With the corrected premise, what is the parity of the sum of the odd-degree vertices?
items.attempt: Each edge has two endpoints, so the sum of all vertex degrees equals the number of edges $|E|$. Suppose the number of odd-degree vertices is odd; then a sum of an odd number of odd numbers is odd, and adding the even sum of the even-degree vertices is still odd, but $|E|$ could be even — a contradiction. So the number of odd-degree vertices is even. Is my reasoning correct?
items.planted_error: The sum of degrees should be 2|E| (each edge contributes 2), not |E|; and "|E| could be even" yields no contradiction — the argument works precisely because the total always equals 2|E| and is thus even, so the original reasoning is logically incomplete.

items.reply: Start from the definition of linear dependence: if $c_1v_1+c_2v_2=0$, what do you want to prove?
Writing it yourself is what will make you remember it. Starting from $c_1v_1+c_2v_2=0$, which quantity would you like to eliminate first?
The argument is circular: "nonzero vectors are linearly independent" is exactly what you're trying to prove. What extra hypothesis does the reference proof add to make the argument valid?
items.attempt: $v_1,v_2$ are eigenvectors, so by definition both are nonzero. Since both vectors are nonzero, the linear combination $c_1v_1+c_2v_2=0$ has only the solution $c_1=c_2=0$, so they are linearly independent. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: "Nonzero vectors must be linearly independent" is false (when v_2=2v_1 both are nonzero yet linearly dependent); the argument never uses the key condition lambda_1 != lambda_2 — an unused hypothesis usually signals a gap.

items.reply: The condition $T^2=0$ means applying $T$ twice gives zero. What does that say about every vector $v$: where does $Tv$ end up?
Writing it yourself is what will make you remember it. First: for any $v\in V$, where does $Tv$ end up?
The direction is backwards: $T^2=0$ gives $\operatorname{Im}(T)\subseteq\ker(T)$, not the reverse. Which inclusion does the reference proof establish first?
items.attempt: $T^2=0$ means the kernel is contained in the image, i.e. $\ker(T)\subseteq\operatorname{Im}(T)$, so $\operatorname{nullity}(T)\le\operatorname{rank}(T)$. By rank-nullity $\operatorname{rank}+\operatorname{nullity}=n$, giving $\operatorname{rank}(T)\ge\dfrac n2$. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: The inclusion direction is reversed: T^2=0 gives Im(T) subset of Ker(T) (any Tv is sent to 0 by T), not Ker subset of Im; so the conclusion's inequality is also reversed (correct is rank <= n/2).

items.reply: Start from an eigenpair $Av=\lambda v$. To show $\lambda$ is real, what kind of quantity would you compute involving $v^*$?

Writing it yourself is what will make you remember it. Here's the first step: if $Av=\lambda v$, left-multiplying by $v^*$ gives $v^*Av=\lambda v^*v$. What must you prove about the two sides before concluding $\lambda$ is real?
The denominator is real and positive, so the ratio is real — that part is fine. But why is $v^TAv$ real?
items.attempt: Suppose $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$. Left-multiply both sides by $v^T$ to get $v^TAv=\lambda v^Tv$. Since $v^Tv=\|v\|^2>0$ and $v^TAv$ is a real number, $\lambda=\dfrac{v^TAv}{v^Tv}$ is real. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: The eigenvector v may be complex: v^Tv is not necessarily ||v||^2 and can be 0 or complex (e.g. v=(1,i)^T gives v^Tv=0), and v^TAv need not be real. One must use the conjugate transpose v* and first argue that v*Av equals its own conjugate.
